Also known as Calvinism, this 16th-century Protestant branch stresses biblical authority, God's sovereignty, and covenant theology as articulated by John Calvin — what movement is this?
Nicknamed 'Captain Comeback,' this Naval Academy grad won the 1963 Heisman Trophy, served a tour in Vietnam, then led the Dallas Cowboys to two Super Bowl titles — who is he?
Roger Staubach: American football player and Navy officer (born 1942)
A Kurdish commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty and became the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria, he led the Muslim effort during the Third Crusade — who is he?
Saladin: Founder of the Ayyubid dynasty (c. 1137–1193)

Considered history's largest colonial campaign, this 1935–36 conflict saw two hundred thousand invading troops attack without a declaration, retaking a town that symbolized their army's earlier defeat there four decades before. Which conflict?
Second Italo-Ethiopian War: 1935–1936 war between Italy and Ethiopia.
Grandson of a prime minister and the longest-serving PM in his nation's history, this Japanese politician led the Liberal Democratic Party across two stints in office — who was he?
Shinzo Abe: Prime Minister of Japan (2006–2007; 2012–2020)
The only communist state ever to exist in the Arab world, this nation in southern Arabia had its capital at Aden before unifying with its northern neighbor in 1990 — what was it?
South Yemen: 1967–1990 state in Western Asia.
Around 986 he revolted against his father Harald Bluetooth to seize Denmark's throne, and in December 1013 briefly became King of England too — which Viking ruler was it?
Swein Forkbeard: King of Denmark and England (died 1014)
Central to Judaism and recounted every Passover, this founding narrative describes the Israelites' escape from Egyptian bondage through a parting of the Red Sea under Moses — what is it?
The Exodus: Founding myth of the Jewish people.
As first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition from 1478, this Dominican friar was also a chief supporter of the decree expelling Jews from Spain — who was he?
Tomás de Torquemada: Grand Inquisitor of Spain (1420–1498)
Often called "Sardar," meaning chief, this Gandhian lawyer became India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, steering the country's political integration — who was he?
This American divorcée's romance with Britain's king forced his abdication in 1936 rather than let her become queen — who was she?
Wallis Simpson: Wife of Prince Edward, Duke of Windsor (1896–1986)

One of three brothers with distinguished military careers, this British general rose to Commander-in-Chief, America, during the War of Independence after famously scaling the cliffs at Quebec in 1759. Who was he?
William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe: British Army officer and politician (1729–1814)

Rooted in pre-Islamic Kurdish tradition and shaped by Sufi influence, this monotheistic faith reveres a 'Peacock Angel' as chief among seven angels tasked with guarding the world — which religion is it?
The eldest child of Alfred the Great, this Anglo-Saxon noblewoman ruled the Mercians in her own right from 911 until her death in 918 — who was she?
Æthelflæd: Ruler of Mercia in England from 911 to 918.
Which of these four was born earliest?
John Ray (born 1627) is the earliest of the four. John Ray (29 November 1627 – 17 January 1705) was an English Christian naturalist and one of the earliest English parson-naturalists.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Marie Curie is a physicist. Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
Which one below is best known as a chemist?
Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim is a chemist. Mai Thi Nguyen-Kim is a German chemist, science communicator, television presenter and YouTuber.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was Carl Linnaeus born?
Carl Linnaeus: Linnaeus was the son of a curate and was born in Råshult, in the countryside of Småland, southern Sweden.
In what year was Bernard Arnault born?
Bernard Arnault: Bernard Jean Étienne Arnault (born 5 March 1949) is a French businessman.
In what year was Jens Stoltenberg born?
Jens Stoltenberg was born in Oslo to diplomat and politician Thorvald Stoltenberg and politician Karin Stoltenberg (née Heiberg).
In what year did Jim Lovell die?
Jim Lovell: James Arthur Lovell Jr. (LUV-əl; March 25, 1928 – August 7, 2025) was an American astronaut, naval aviator, test pilot, and mechanical engineer.
In what year did Werner Heisenberg die?
Werner Heisenberg: Heisenberg published his Umdeutung paper in 1925, a major reinterpretation of old quantum theory.
In what year was Uranium discovered?
Uranium is a chemical element; it has symbol U and atomic number 92.
In what year was Cobalt discovered?
Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Ciprofloxacin: Pfizer. Ciprofloxacin, sold under the brand name Cipro among others, is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a number of bacterial infections.
Which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 from?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Soviet Union. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Who is credited with discovering Tucana?
Tucana: Petrus Plancius. Tucana (The Toucan) is a constellation in the southern sky, named after the toucan, a South American bird.
Who is credited with discovering Cro-Magnon?
Cro-Magnon: Louis Lartet. Cro-Magnons produced Upper Palaeolithic cultures, the first major one being the Aurignacian, which was succeeded by the Gravettian by 30,000 years ago.
Who is credited with discovering Makemake?
Makemake: Michael E. Brown. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, this family of hook-billed raptors includes buzzards, vultures, and kites across 75 genera — which family is this?
Accipitridae is one of the four families within the order Accipitriformes, and is a family of small to large birds of prey with strongly hooked bills and variable morphology based on diet.
This English academic and broadcaster, an anatomist and archaeologist by training, was president of the charity Humanists UK from 2019 to 2022 — who is she?
Alice Roberts (born 19 May 1973) is an English academic, anatomist, archaeologist, TV presenter and author.

Native to tropical America and carried across the Pacific by Spanish traders aboard the Manila galleons, this small tree in the same family as soursop produces a scaly-skinned fruit with sweet, creamy flesh — what's the species?
Annona squamosa is a small, well-branched tree or shrub from the family Annonaceae that bears edible fruits called sugar apples or sweetsops or custard apples.
Named from Greek words for 'even' and 'toe,' this mammal order bears its weight equally on two of its five toes, unlike its odd-toed counterpart — what order is it?
Artiodactyla (from Ancient Greek rtios 'even' and dktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.
Native to Europe, this small white-petaled, yellow-centered lawn flower is called 'common,' 'lawn,' or 'English' in various regions — what is its scientific name?
Bellis perennis (p-), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
Recognised by South Africa's Kennel Union but not by the international federation, this large, muscular mastiff-type breed serves as a family guard dog — name it?
Boerboel is a South African breed of large dog of mastiff type, used as a family guard dog.
This English-like, compiled programming language was designed for business use and remains widely used today to maintain legacy mainframe systems in banking and government — what language is it?
COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which metabolic process is the polar opposite of anabolism, breaking large molecules such as proteins and lipids down into monomers while releasing energy, some of it lost as heat?
Catabolism is the set of metabolic pathways that breaks down molecules into smaller units that are either oxidized to release energy or used in other anabolic reactions.
The first element in group 6, it lends its name to the shiny plating on car bumpers and, mixed into steel, makes it stainless. Which steely-grey metal is it?
Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
Known in the US as 'konk,' this sea snail's family includes so-called 'true' species identified by their long spires — what is it?
Conch is any of a number of different medium-to-large-sized sea snails.
This term describes all the material inside a cell's outer membrane, excluding the nucleus (in cells that have one) — its main components include a gel-like fluid called the cytosol. What is it?
Cytoplasm is all the material within a eukaryotic or prokaryotic cell, enclosed by the cell membrane, including the organelles and excluding the nucleus in eukaryotic cells.

Bred in the early twentieth century in Córdoba, Argentina, for hunting big game like wild boar and pumas, this large mastiff-type dog breed traces its ancestry partly to a now-extinct fighting dog — name the breed?
Dogo Argentino (plural Dogos Argentinos) is an Argentine breed of large dog of mastiff type.
Many of these Northern Hemisphere shade trees, prized along old European and American streets, were wiped out by a fungus carried by bark beetles — which tree genus is this?
Elm are deciduous and semi-deciduous trees comprising the genus Ulmus in the family Ulmaceae.

The telltale earth mounds this tunneling mammal pushes to the surface come from its constantly expanding burrow system, and it feeds mainly on earthworms paralyzed by toxins in its saliva — what animal is it?
European mole (Talpa europaea) is a mammal of the order Eulipotyphla.

This genetic neurodevelopmental disorder causes a long, narrow face, large ears, and unusually flexible fingers, with males typically far more affected than females and average IQ under 55 in affected boys — what's the condition?

Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. The average IQ in males with FXS is under 55, while affected females tend to be in the borderline to normal range, typically around 70–85.

This heavy, slow-moving reptile native to the southwestern US and northwestern Mexico is the only venomous lizard found in the United States, though its sluggish nature makes it rarely dangerous — what animal is it?
Gila monster (Heloderma suspectum) is a species of venomous lizard native to the Southwestern United States and the northwestern Mexican state of Sonora.
This eel-shaped ocean scavenger defends itself by flooding predators with slime from glands in its skin — what creature is it?
Hagfish (also known as Hyperotreti) and order Myxiniformes, are eel-shaped jawless fish (occasionally called slime eels).

Discovered in 2013 deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this archaic human left behind over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, yet a tiny brain keeps its place in our family tree a puzzle — what species is it?

Homo naledi is an extinct species of archaic human discovered in 2013 in the Rising Star Cave system, Gauteng province, South Africa, part of the Cradle of Humankind, dating back to the Middle Pleistocene 335,000-236,000 years ago.
Aided by Soviet intelligence gathered on the American Manhattan Project, this physicist oversaw the first Soviet nuclear weapon test at Semipalatinsk in 1949 — who is he?
Igor Kurchatov was Soviet nuclear physicist (1903–1960).
The first woman ever to chair the Federal Reserve, she later became the first woman to serve as U.S. Treasury secretary — a Brooklyn-born, Yale-trained economist. Who is she?
Janet Yellen (born August 13, 1946) is an American economist who served as the 78th United States secretary of the treasury from 2021 to 2025 and as chair of the Federal Reserve from 2014 to 2018.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.
This small Arctic rodent is a key prey source for tundra carnivores and is the subject of a persistent myth that it marches off cliffs in mass suicide — what animal is it?
Lemming is a small rodent, usually found in or near the Arctic in tundra biomes.
This evergreen tree, native to the cooler hills of south-central China, is grown commercially for its orange fruit and is sometimes called the Japanese medlar. What is it?
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica) is a large evergreen shrub or tree grown commercially for its orange coloured fruits.
This computer scientist led the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer and is credited with coining the very term 'software engineering' — who is she?
Margaret Hamilton (software engineer) (ne Heafield; born August 17, 1936) is an American computer scientist.
This medication treats nausea, vomiting, and acid reflux by blocking dopamine receptors, but is rarely recommended for more than twelve weeks due to a risk of movement disorders — what drug is it?
Metoclopramide is a medication used to treat nausea, vomiting, gastroparesis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease.
This Bangladeshi economist pioneered microcredit and founded Grameen Bank, work that earned him the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before he later led an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus (born 28 June 1940) is a Bangladeshi economist and statesman.

Discovered in a fossil-rich West African formation and first described in 1976 but not formally named until 1999, this rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur lived roughly 115 to 105 million years ago — which genus?
Nigersaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived during the middle Cretaceous period, about 115 to 105 million years ago.
This flowering herb in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean, is sometimes called wild marjoram and is a staple of countless savory dishes. What is it?
Oregano (Origanum vulgare) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
This New York Times columnist of 24 years was the sole winner of the 2008 Nobel in economics for explaining the patterns of international trade and where economic activity clusters. Who is he?
Paul Krugman (born February 28, 1953) is an American economist who is the Distinguished Professor of Economics at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York.

This branch of linguistics studies how languages organize their foundational sound units — like the contrast between 'bat' and 'gnat' — or, in sign languages, elements like hand shape and location — what is it called?
Phonology (formerly also phonemics or phonematics) is the branch of linguistics that concerns how languages organize the foundational elements that make their words.

Native to most of the Northern Hemisphere, this genus of 25 to 30 deciduous tree species includes poplars, aspens, and cottonwoods, one of which was the first tree ever fully DNA-sequenced — which genus?
Populus is a genus of 25-30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere.

Brought from China to Europe in the sixteenth century and popularized by the House of Orange in the Netherlands, this dog breed is known for its wrinkly, short-muzzled face and curled tail — name the breed?
Pug is a breed of dog with the physically distinctive features of a wrinkly, short-muzzled face, and curled tail.
This positive-sense RNA virus in the Enterovirus genus is the most common viral infectious agent in humans and the leading cause of the common cold — name the virus?
Rhinovirus (from the Ancient) is a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Enterovirus in the family Picornaviridae.
This American painter turned inventor co-developed a telegraph system and became the namesake of the dot-dash code that helped make telegraphy commercially viable — who is he?
Samuel Morse (April 27, 1791 - April 2, 1872) was an American inventor and painter.
Before becoming the first woman on Facebook's board, this executive ran global sales at Google and assisted Lawrence Summers at the World Bank — who later wrote 'Lean In'?
Sheryl Sandberg (born August 28, 1969) is an American technology executive, philanthropist and writer.
This leafy green vegetable's high oxalate content gives raw and cooked versions noticeably different flavors, with blanching helping to tone it down — what vegetable is it?
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia.
These large waterfowl of the genus Cygnus are close relatives of geese and ducks, and are known for typically mating for life. What birds are they?
Swan are birds of the genus Cygnus within the family Anatidae.
Classed among the saurischians and placing them nearer to sauropodomorphs than to ornithischians, these hollow-boned, three-toed dinosaurs were ancestrally meat-eaters — which clade?
Theropoda (from ancient Greek -) is one of the three major clades of dinosaur, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha.
One of the earliest arthropod groups ever to appear in the fossil record, this extinct marine creature persisted in the oceans for nearly 270 million years across over 22,000 species — what is it?
Trilobite (meaning "three-lobed entities") are extinct marine arthropods that form the class Trilobita.
Its wild form is dioecious while domesticated versions bear hermaphrodite flowers — this Mediterranean-native plant is the ancestor of nearly all wine and table varieties — what species?

Vitis vinifera is a species of flowering plant, native to the Mediterranean region, Central Europe, and southwestern Asia, from Morocco and Portugal north to southern Germany and east to northern Iran.
Almost always found combined with lanthanide minerals and never on its own in nature, this element with symbol Y is a key ingredient in the phosphors used inside LEDs — which element?
Yttrium is a chemical element; it has symbol Y and atomic number 39.

The only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, this English mathematician saw that Charles Babbage's analytical engine could do far more than crunch numbers — earning her a reputation as the first computer programmer. Who was she?
Shining as the brightest star in Taurus some 67 light-years from Earth, this red giant has swollen to roughly 45 times the Sun's size despite a cooler surface — which star?
Aldebaran: Taurus Brightest Star. Aldebaran (Arabic: الدَّبَرَان, lit. 'The Follower') is a star in the zodiac constellation of Taurus.
Used to treat dangerous heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation, which drug can take weeks to work when swallowed but carries risks of lung, liver, thyroid, and eye toxicity?

Serving as Surveyor of the Queen's Pictures while secretly working as the 'fourth man' of a notorious spy ring, this British art historian wrote a landmark 1967 study of the painter Nicolas Poussin — who is he?
Anthony Blunt: British art historian and Soviet spy (1907–1983)
Pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon in 2003, this mountaineer amputated his own forearm with a dull pocket knife to survive, later portrayed by James Franco in a film — who is he?
Delivered to the RAF starting in 1956, this delta-wing strategic bomber was considered the most advanced but riskiest of Britain's three V bombers — which aircraft?
Avro Vulcan: British jet-powered delta wing strategic bomber.
Nicknamed 'top shelf' dizziness, this inner-ear disorder causes brief spinning sensations lasting under a minute whenever you tilt or turn your head — what is this condition called?
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: Medical condition. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), sometimes called "top shelf vertigo", is a disorder arising from a problem in the inner ear.
This medical term for blood escaping the circulatory system describes a healthy person as able to lose 10 to 15 percent of their total volume without serious harm — what is it called?
Bleeding: Blood escaping from the circulatory system. Bleeding, hemorrhage, haemorrhage or blood loss, is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels.
Making up just 2.6 percent of the brain's weight, this stalk-like structure connects the cerebrum to the spinal cord and houses all ten pairs of cranial nerve origins — what is it?
Brainstem: Posterior part of the brain, adjoining and structurally continuous.
Its Latin name means "chisel-bearing," a nod to the stout egg-laying organs of its members — which insect suborder includes grasshoppers, ground-hoppers, and pygmy mole crickets?
Caelifera: Suborder of insects. The latter should not be confused with the mole crickets (Gryllotalpidae), which belong to the other Orthopteran suborder Ensifera.
A founder of humanistic psychology, this American psychologist pioneered person-centered therapy, an approach that also shaped student-centered learning in education — who is he?
Certified in 1984 and developed into a freighter variant for FedEx, this single-engine turboprop utility plane typically seats nine and can be fitted with floats or skis — which aircraft?
Cessna 208 Caravan: Family of utility transport aircraft.
Blooming in autumn and closely associated with the month of November, this East Asian flowering genus in the daisy family boasts thousands of horticultural varieties — which flower?
Chrysanthemum: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family.

Triggered by an abnormal immune response to gluten found in wheat, barley, and rye, this chronic autoimmune condition mainly affects the small intestine and often causes malabsorption in children — which condition?
Coeliac disease: Autoimmune disorder. Coeliac disease (Commonwealth English) or celiac disease (American English) is a chronic autoimmune disease, mainly affecting the small intestine.
Also known as the Cornelian cherry, this dogwood-family shrub or small tree is native to western and southern Europe as well as southwestern Asia — what's its scientific name?
Cornus mas: Species of flowering plant in the family Cornaceae.
Also called Bermuda grass, this hardy warm-climate turf species is ironically not native to the island of the same name — which plant, by its scientific name?
Cynodon dactylon: Species of grass. Cynodon dactylon, commonly known as Bermuda grass or as couch grass in Australia and New Zealand, is a grass found worldwide in warm and tropical climates.
This central nervous system stimulant is the 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a well-known molecule, prescribed for ADHD and narcolepsy and sometimes given as an inactive prodrug — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine: CNS stimulant and isomer of amphetamine.
A broad-spectrum member of the tetracycline class, this antibiotic treats everything from acne and chlamydia to Lyme disease and cholera — though it'll make you sunburn more easily. Which drug?
Doxycycline: Tetracycline-class antibiotic. It is used to treat bacterial pneumonia, acne, chlamydia infections, Lyme disease, cholera, typhus, and syphilis, and is sometimes used to prevent malaria.
This unit of energy equals the kinetic energy a single electron gains while crossing an electric potential difference of one volt — what is it called?
Sometimes abbreviated ETM, this antibiotic treats everything from respiratory infections to syphilis and is the eye ointment routinely dabbed on newborns to prevent eye infections. What is it?
Erythromycin: Antibiotic medication. Erythromycin (sometimes abbreviated ETM in reports) is an antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
Native to the Iberian Peninsula and introduced to hundreds of locations worldwide, this grassland herbivore digs extensive burrow networks called warrens — what is it?
Found on the forelimbs of most tetrapods, these prehensile, often opposable digits give primates like humans their dexterity for grasping and fine movement — what are they called?

This German chemist won a Nobel Prize for inventing a process that synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gas — a breakthrough that today supports nearly half the world's food production. Who is he?

Working at Tuskegee Institute, this agricultural scientist urged cotton farmers to plant peanuts and sweet potatoes instead, publishing dozens of practical bulletins to fight soil depletion. Who is he?
George Washington Carver: American botanist and inventor (1864–1943)
This inflammatory arthritis brings on rapid, searing pain — often in the joint at the base of the big toe — caused by needle-shaped crystals of uric acid building up in the blood. What is it?
Gout: Form of arthritis causing swollen joints.
Its name literally combines words for 'holy' and 'flatfish,' reflecting its popularity on Catholic holy days — this demersal fish is prized both as food and as a sport catch. Which fish?
This German-American statistician patented an electromechanical punched-card tabulating machine in 1884, founding a company that would eventually be renamed IBM — who was he?
Herman Hollerith: American statistician and inventor. Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company.

This fatal inherited neurodegenerative disorder, once called a 'chorea,' starts with subtle mood changes before bringing on uncoordinated, dance-like involuntary movements as the basal ganglia degrade — what is it?
Huntington's disease: Inherited neurodegenerative disorder. Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Formed by the merger of two hip flexor muscles that join at the femur's lesser trochanter, this is the body's strongest flexor of the hip — what is it called?
Iliopsoas: Joined psoas and iliacus muscles of the hip and thigh.
Native to Africa and Eurasia, this opportunistic canid can sustain a running pace of about 10 mph over long distances while hunting small mammals, birds, and reptiles — which animal?
As a Princeton grad student this mathematician dreamed up an "equilibrium" concept that won him a 1994 Nobel in Economics — who was he?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: American mathematician and Nobel Laureate (1928–2015)
Smaller, seedier, and more aromatic than its Persian cousin, this citrus hybrid lends its tart flavor to a beloved Florida pie named after the island chain it's associated with — what is it?
Key lime: Citrus fruit and plant.
Described both as a science and as the art of justice, this set of enforced rules can be made by legislatures, executive decrees or judges' precedent — what is it?
A sweet, aromatic flavouring used in confectionery, tobacco, and pharmaceuticals comes from the root of which legume — though more than a couple of milligrams per kilo a day can cause trouble?
Often a complication of cancer treatment, this incurable, progressive swelling condition is managed with compression therapy and manual drainage rather than diuretics — what is it?
Lymphedema: Swelling due to a compromised lymphatic system.

The first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed as a university math professor, this Milanese scholar later traded calculus for four decades of theology and charity — who is she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi: Italian mathematician and philanthropist (1718–1799)
Typically running 21 to 35 days, this coordinated dance of estrogen and progesterone prepares the uterine lining and releases an egg to make pregnancy possible — what is it?
Menstrual cycle: Natural changes in the human female reproductive system.

Soviet pilots called it the "Balalaika" because its planform looked like the stringed instrument, while Poles dubbed it "Ołówek" — the pencil — for its slender fuselage; which most-produced supersonic jet in history earned all those nicknames?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: 1956 Soviet fighter aircraft family.
Native to northern India, this fast-growing, drought-resistant tree is nicknamed the 'drumstick tree' for its seed pods and the 'horseradish tree' for its pungent roots — what is it?
Moringa oleifera: Species of flowering tree.
Made of two fused benzene rings, this pungent white crystalline compound is the main ingredient in traditional mothballs — what is it?
Naphthalene: Chemical compound. It is a white crystalline solid with a characteristic odor that is detectable at concentrations as low as 0.08 ppm.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, who endowed a famous set of prizes — fitting, since this synthetic metal can only be forged in particle accelerators. What is it?
Nobelium: Chemical element with atomic number 102 (No)
Causing white or yellow discoloration, thickening, and lifting of the nail — and far more often striking toenails than fingernails — what is this fungal infection also called tinea unguium?
Named by Reginald Innes Pocock in 1917 to cover big cats of genus Panthera, this cat subfamily later grew to include the clouded leopards too — which subfamily?
Pantherinae: Subfamily of felids. The Pantherinae genetically diverged from a common ancestor between 9.32 to 4.47 million years ago and 10.67 to 3.76 million years ago.
Harvested from Penicillium moulds and brewed in deep tanks, this β-lactam was among the first medicines to knock out staph and strep infections. What is it?
Penicillin: Group of antibiotics derived from fungi.

So reactive that it never appears uncombined in nature, this element was famously isolated in 1669 by Hennig Brand — the scientific community's first documented discovery of an element — and comes in white and red forms. Which one is it?
Phosphorus: Chemical element with atomic number 15 (P)
This plant process moves pollen from an anther to a stigma, eventually letting a tube grow down the style to reach the ovary and enable fertilization. What is it?
Pollination: Biological process occurring in plants.
Discovered in 1915, this red dwarf is the closest star to Earth besides the Sun, orbiting its two larger neighbors once every 550,000 years — which star?
Proxima Centauri: Nearest star to the Solar System.
Used to treat malaria resistant to chloroquine, this bitter compound also flavors tonic water and can cause ringing in the ears at high doses — what is it?
Quinine: Medication used to treat malaria and babesiosis.
With the widest geographic range of any non-human primate, this brown-to-grey Old World monkey lives in matrilineal troops of up to 200 individuals — which species?
Rhesus macaque: Species of Old World monkey. The rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta), colloquially rhesus monkey, is a species of Old World monkey in the Macaca genus.
What term describes herbivorous mammals like cattle and giraffes that digest plant matter by regurgitating and re-chewing it as cud?
Ruminant: Hoofed herbivorous grazing or browsing mammals.
About 90% of cases trace to a herniated spinal disc pressing on a nerve root, producing a shooting pain that runs from the lower back down one leg — what's the condition?
Sciatica: Lower-back pain that can extend down the leg.
Nicknamed the 'brushwood dog' for its game-flushing hunting style, this is the smallest of Japan's six native dog breeds — which breed?
Shiba Inu: Japanese dog breed. The Shiba Inu (Japanese: 柴犬; Japanese pronunciation: [ɕi.ba.i.nɯ]) is a breed of hunting dog from Japan.

Originating in South America and rapidly diversifying after the extinction of the dinosaurs, this plant family — commonly known as the nightshades — includes toxic alkaloid-rich species alongside tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers. What family is it?
Built from four fused carbon rings, this class of organic compounds includes cholesterol, testosterone, and anabolic performance-enhancers — what is it called?
Steroid: Polycyclic organic compound having sterane as a core structure.

Caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously hides: a painless ulcer first, then a rash that loves the palms and soles, then years of silent latency before tertiary damage. What is it?
